name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5
lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold under the trade name Syn-Coll, is a synthetic lipopeptide used as an ingredient in anti-wrinkle and skin-firming cosmetics. It is marketed as a "signal peptide" intended to prompt skin cells to make more collagen, and it appears in creams, serums and microneedle patches.

Published material on the ingredient is sparse. A clinical study of hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several bioactive peptides evaluated tolerability and skin effects of a multi-peptide product [1], and laboratory work has used it as a component of collagen nanoparticle formulations [4]. No published trial appears to isolate palmitoyl tripeptide-5 as a single active against placebo.

paras: The peptide is used in cosmetic products aimed at fine lines and loss of firmness. Manufacturers describe it as stimulating collagen production through a growth-factor-related signalling pathway (marketed as TGF-beta stimulation); these mechanism statements originate largely from supplier material rather than independent trials.

A monocentric clinical study examined hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with a combination of bioactive peptides in ageing skin, assessing dermal tolerability and effects on skin parameters [1]. Because the patch contained several actives and used a microneedle delivery system, the results cannot be attributed to palmitoyl tripeptide-5 alone. A 2025 laboratory study combined lactoferrin, recombinant human collagen and palmitoyl tripeptide-5 in nanoparticles and reported anti-wrinkle, moisturising and whitening effects in experimental models [4]. A registered trial of Hydrafacial treatments listed skin quality and hydration outcomes in 27 adults [5]; the registration does not by itself show a specific effect of this peptide.
No specific adverse-effect literature for the peptide was identified. General reviews of cosmetic peptides discuss their use in formulations for sensitive skin [2].

card.summary: A collagen-signalling cosmetic peptide (Syn-Coll) with only multi-ingredient, small-scale evidence behind it.
card.note: Evidence comes from multi-ingredient products; no isolated placebo-controlled trial found.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 is a lab-made peptide attached to a fatty acid, added to anti-ageing creams and serums. It is marketed as telling skin cells to produce more collagen.

Published evidence is thin: studies have tested it mixed with other ingredients, and no standalone placebo-controlled human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: Suppliers say it acts as a signal peptide that stimulates collagen synthesis via a TGF-beta-related pathway; the fatty chain is intended to help it cross the outer skin layer. This is mainly manufacturer description.
quick.risks: No specific safety problems are documented in the sources found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
